title: The banyan deer
hookLine: a deer king takes the place of a pregnant doe; the hunting king is moved to stop the hunt (Jataka 12)

lines: A KING WHO LOVED TO HUNT.
cards: Have you ever taken someone's shift so they could be at a birth, or a funeral, or just sleep? Somebody's turn was coming, and you stepped in.
In the days when Brahmadatta ruled Benares, the story goes, the king loved to hunt deer, and every day he dragged the townspeople out of their fields to help.
Tired of it, the people drove a whole forest of deer into the king's park, shut the gate, and said: there. Hunt them there. In that park were two herds, each with its own king.
One was a golden deer called Banyan, our hero. The other was called Branch.

teach.h: A GRIM DEAL: ONE A DAY.
teach.b: Every day the king or his cook came and shot at the deer, and many were wounded in the chaos, not just the one taken. So Banyan went to Branch with a grim deal: let's draw lots.
One deer each day goes to the chopping block on its own, and the herds take turns. Fewer will suffer. The king, who admired the two golden deer, had already promised never to kill their leaders.
One day the lot falls on a doe in Branch's herd who is about to give birth. Let me have my fawn first, she asks her king, and then I'll go.
Branch refuses: it's your turn. Go. So she goes to Banyan.
I'll take your turn. He walks to the block and lays his head on it. The cook runs to tell the king, who comes and says: I spared you.
Why are you here? The deer explains about the doe, and the king is moved beyond words. I have never seen such kindness, even among people, he says.
Get up. I spare your life and hers. And the rest of the deer?
Banyan asks. Them too. And the other animals in the forest?
Them too. And the birds? The fish in the water?
One by one, the deer king asks, until every creature has been given its safety.
Tradition says this was one of the Buddha's earlier lives. The Jataka's closing verse boils down to this: better to stay close to Banyan than to live with Branch.

how: The banyan deer story is told in Buddhist schools and temples to illustrate compassion and self-sacrifice.

o: a mountain lion who ruled the hills
a forest hermit who lived among the deer
a golden deer king named for the banyan tree

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: the golden deer king who stood in
the king who said: it's your turn

s: Banyan was forced to go to the block
the king had promised to spare him. he went in the doe's place.
the deer king kept asking until every creature was safe
the deer, the forest animals, the birds, the fish.
the doe's own king agreed to let her wait
Branch refused. Banyan said: go home, I'll take your turn.

games.q: you're the doe. your turn has come, and your fawn is about to be born. your own king has refused you. what do you do?
games.why: she asks Banyan. he tells her to go home, and lays his own head on the block.

practice: Think of who around you is carrying something heavy right now: a new parent, a worn-out coworker, a friend with a sick relative.
Picture one of them, and yourself stepping in for one small thing, the dishes, the school run, a phone call they dread. You don't have to lay your head on a block; one turn is enough.

wordCard.voice: Nigrodha. The banyan deer, a golden deer king who took a pregnant doe's turn at the block, and moved a hunting king to spare every creature.

orig.note: Pali: the banyan tree. The story is the Nigrodhamiga Jataka, the banyan deer.

carryVoice: Your line: stand in for someone. One turn taken, and safety for every creature. That's day eighty-six.
